statement: The draft is a solid base. Decisions, denials, mocks and secret injection are all first-class events, and dropping ActorIdentified is acceptable only if every event envelope requires actor, on-behalf-of chain, shell CID and cause. What is missing is mostly the back half of records management: a hold is placed but never released, an erasure happens without a request or a refusal, retention is one event that mixes the rule with the purge, and we cannot prove verification ran. Some events also read as if history can be undone ('Reverted', 'Upcasted'). I want every one of them to be a forward-only fact that points at earlier facts.

renames.why: At run start, record everything needed to reconstruct the run: program CID, resolved package CIDs, shell CID, workspace config CID and file system root. 'References' sounds like packages only, and a run without its pinned shell and config cannot be re-evaluated later.

Upcasting on read changes no state, so it is not an event. Registering the upcaster (its CID, who approved it, which schema versions it maps) does change how history is read, and that is the fact an auditor needs.

merges.why: A revert is a new version whose source equals an earlier CID, with a 'restores' field and a reason. A separate 'Reverted' event suggests history was undone. It was not, and effects already performed stand (see H20).

splits.why: The rule (who set which period for which scope, under what legal basis) and the execution (which events or blocks were purged, up to which position, with a tombstone hash) are evidenced separately. A purge must reference the policy version it applied.

When a gate changes what the program asked for, that is a policy act in its own right. Auditors filter on it ('show me every time policy altered an agent's request'), and it must carry both the original and the rewritten input digests.

missing.why: Positive evidence that the chain was checked from position A to B against a signed checkpoint. TamperDetected alone proves nothing when it never fires.
A hold without a release has no lifecycle. Who lifted it, on whose authority and when retention resumes must all be recorded.
Erasure has a legal deadline that starts at the request. Request, refusal and completion are distinct facts, with the data subject and the scope.
When a hold and an erasure request conflict, the outcome and its basis must be on record, not resolved silently.
Offboarding: the person's tokens, bindings and shell are withdrawn, while their past events stay attributed to them.
Slack, Discord or WhatsApp edits and deletions arrive later. We record that the source changed, without rewriting the original MessagePosted.
Sharing exposes data outside the channel. The window of exposure needs both its start and its end.

context_changes.change: Split audit into 'evidence' (the global hash-chained ledger, checkpoints, verification, export, projection rebuilds, upcaster registry) and 'records management' (retention policies, purges, legal holds, erasure requests and outcomes).
context_changes.why: Evidence is technical and must never be bypassed. Records management is a governed process with approvals and legal deadlines, which only ever acts through evidence by appending tombstones. Keeping them apart stops 'retention' from becoming a back door that rewrites the log.

hotspot_positions.position: Keep separate events (EffectPermitted, EffectInputRewrittenByGate, EffectMocked, EffectDenied, GateFailed) sharing a common envelope: run id, effect label, input digest, shell CID, gate CID, actor chain. Separate names make denials and mocks first-class in queries and exports. A single EffectDecided with a field invites projections that only look at the happy path.

Replay uses the recorded decisions, because that is what actually happened. Anything not yet journaled is decided against the shell in force now. A revocation between the two is recorded explicitly (the next decision cites the newer shell CID), so the record shows exactly when authority ended.

Never silently retry a non-idempotent effect. Record EffectOutcomeInDoubt, reconcile against the platform where possible (EffectReconciled, citing the evidence), and otherwise ask a person, whose answer is an attributed event.

Every effect result is journaled, Now and Random included, because they decide behaviour and I must be able to reproduce it. Durability (fsync before resume) can be relaxed per effect class only for effects with no external side effect, and the shell or workspace must state that choice as configuration that is itself versioned.

EffectMocked is its own event and carries the mocked value's digest and the gate CID. Every projection and export marks results derived from a mock, and replay feeds the same mock rather than performing the real effect.

Keep personal data out of event envelopes. Payloads go to the block store, encrypted with a per-subject key, and the event holds only the CID plus a plaintext hash. Erasure destroys the key (crypto-shredding) and appends a tombstone, so the chain stays verifiable and the content becomes unreadable. A legal hold blocks key destruction.

One stream per aggregate for consistency, plus a single global append position per cloud that is hash chained (each entry commits to its predecessor and to the aggregate event hash). The authoritative 'when' is the ledger's append time at the global position. The Now effect value and platform timestamps are recorded as claims, not as ordering.

Agree: never rewrite stored events. Upcasters are pure EYG functions referenced by CID and registered via EventUpcasterRegistered, so a reader can prove which transformation produced a view. Exports include the raw events alongside the upcasted view.

Agree, and make it explicit: tracing is a debugging view derived from the ledger (or a lossy sidecar). Nothing in compliance may rely on traces. OTLP export dropping spans is acceptable only because it is not the record.

Redact at the effect boundary using the declared secret names: record the hash placeholder and secret version, never the value. SetSecret's event carries the name, version and fingerprint. A replay that needs the value fetches the current secret version, and if that version has been rotated away, the replay must stop rather than substitute.
Agree: RunBasisPinned records the resolved CID for every @name, along with the signature that was verified. Replay and audit only ever use pinned CIDs.

Payloads go to blobs by CID. Roots that keep blocks alive are: live file system roots, events within retention, and any scope under legal hold. Garbage collection must consult holds and emit what it removed, and a purge of held content is impossible by construction.

The envelope has mandatory fields: actor {kind: person|agent|trigger|schedule|connection|system, id}, on_behalf_of (an ordered chain ending in a person or the workspace configuration version), shell CID and causation id. Events missing them are rejected at append. A trigger's authority is the person who added it plus the channel shell CID at the time the trigger fired.

CloudBootstrapped records the first admin with the operator's out-of-band proof (a one-time setup token). 'First visitor becomes admin' must go. Sign-in by name only is not attributable and fails audit.

Both are events. A runtime trigger is TriggerAdded attributed to its actor, and TriggerSavedToWorkspace is a configuration change. When they conflict, the workspace configuration wins, and the overridden runtime trigger gets a TriggerStopped event giving the reason, so nothing disappears silently.

Unauthenticated connections are allowed only by explicit, attributed configuration (UnauthenticatedConnectionCreated, with who accepted the risk). Every event they deliver is marked unauthenticated in projections. Replayed deliveries are recorded as rejected duplicates, never dropped silently.

Record a digest-level receipt for every delivery (source, delivery id, payload CID). Payload retention can be short by policy, but whenever an event matched a trigger or reached a run, its payload is retained as long as that run's evidence.

Statements that change data are events (with statement text, parameter digests, actor, run). The SQLite file is a projection that can be rebuilt, and periodic DatabaseSnapshotTaken events carry its CID so past table states can be reconstructed without replaying from the beginning.
Whichever rule a schedule uses (I lean towards one catch-up fire by default), every missed occurrence must be recorded as CronOccurrenceMissed, with the reason (downtime) and what was done instead.

Revert means a new configuration version equal to an older CID. Effects already performed are facts and stay. The revert event cites the reason and the version it restores, and if compensation is needed, it is a new, attributed run.

new_hotspots.text: Who holds the key that signs audit checkpoints, and can the same operator who runs the cloud also sign? I want checkpoints anchored outside the operator's control (e.g. published to the hub or a third party) so a compromised admin cannot re-sign a rewritten log.
Four-eyes approval: retention changes, legal hold release, erasure and shell changes that widen agent permissions. Should these require a second person's approval event before taking effect?

We need a read model 'policy in force at time T' for any actor: the shell CID, which gates it contained and which workspace configuration granted it. Without it, 'what was this agent allowed to do last March' cannot be answered quickly.
Legal holds against content-addressed deduplication: one block can belong to both held and unheld scopes. Should erasure destroy it, keep it, or re-encrypt it per scope?
